query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor fraction of silicon carbide (SiC) as a reactive sintering aid in ZrB2 processing will enable densification at lower temperatures while simultaneously forming protective intergranular phases that enhance oxidation durability and resistance to liquid plating metal corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Single‐phase ZrB2 typically prepared at high temperatures (above 2300 °C) with a dense network of Zr–B and B–B bonds but prone to oxidation and liquid metal corrosion when processed at reduced temperatures.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a controlled low weight percentage (e.g., 5–10 wt%) of SiC into the ZrB2 powder and process via reactive liquid phase–assisted spark plasma sintering at reduced temperatures (~1800–2000 °C).
generation.conditions: Sintering under controlled atmospheres to limit contaminants, targeting processing temperatures between 1800 and 2000 °C with subsequent service in high-temperature oxidizing environments and exposure to liquid plating metal baths.
generation.structural_mediator: The addition of SiC promotes the formation of a transient, eutectic liquid phase at the grain boundaries, leading to enhanced densification and the development of a robust intergranular network that can form stable, protective oxides during service.
generation.mechanism: SiC acts as a sintering aid by lowering the effective processing temperature through reactive liquid phase formation, while its reaction by-products at the interfaces help seal grain boundaries, reduce pathways for oxygen ingress, and inhibit corrosive attack by liquid metals.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventional high-temperature sintered single‐phase ZrB2 and previously attempted lower-temperature specimens, the SiC-doped composite is expected to exhibit improved densification and strength, better preservation of structural integrity, and a significant improvement in oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: Traditional single‐phase ZrB2 prepared above 2300 °C or lower‐temperature specimens that, while processed at reduced temperatures, remain vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated when the SiC content is kept low (e.g., below 10 wt%) to avoid phase segregation and when the sintering temperature is maintained between 1800 °C and 2000 °C; performance may differ outside these limits.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal SiC fraction and sintering parameters require experimental optimization; potential deleterious reactions at the interface or formation of unwanted secondary phases could counteract the benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of ZrB2 with 5–10 wt% SiC and a control set of pure ZrB2, both processed via spark plasma sintering at temperatures between 1800 and 2000 °C under identical conditions. Evaluate the microstructure, densification, mechanical properties, oxidation behavior at high temperatures, and corrosion performance in a liquid plating-metal bath.
measurements: Density and porosity via Archimedes’ method and SEM imaging
Phase and microstructural analysis using XRD and TEM
Mechanical properties (hardness, fracture toughness, and strength)
Oxidation kinetics (weight gain/loss measurements) and corrosion rates in a simulated liquid metal environment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SiC-doped samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in densification, mechanical strength, and resistance to oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion compared to both the high-temperature pure ZrB2 and previously reported lower-temperature specimens, then the hypothesis is falsified.

High-Entropy Diborides—Silicon Carbide Composites by Reactive and Non-Reactive Spark Plasma Sintering: A Comparative Study

Abstract: AbstractThe reactive spark plasma sintering (R-SPS) method was compared in this work with the two-step SHS–SPS route, based on the combination of the self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) with the SPS process, for the fabrication of dense (Hf0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2)B2–SiC and (Hf0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2Ta0.2Zr0.2)B2–SiC ceramics. A multiphase and inhomogeneous product, containing various borides, was obtained at 2000 °C/20 min by R-SPS from transition metals, B4C, and Si. In contrast, if the same precursors were first reacted by SHS and then processed by SPS under the optimized condition of 1800 °C/20 min, the desired ceramics were successfully attained. The resulting sintered samples possessed relative densities above 97% and displayed uniform microstructures with residual oxide content <2.4 wt.%. The presence of SiC made the sintering temperature milder, i.e., 150 °C below that needed by the corresponding additive-free system. Rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering of high-entropy ceramic composites

Abstract: High-entropy ceramics and their composites display high mechanical strength and attractive high-temperature stabilities. However, properties like strong covalent bond character and low self-diffusion coefficients make them difficult to get sintered, limiting their mass popularity. Here, we present a rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering strategy and use high-entropy metal diboride/boron carbide composite as a proof of concept. We use a carbon-based heater to fast-heat the composite to around 3000 K, and a small fraction of eutectic liquid was formed at the interface between high-entropy metal diborides and boron carbide. A crystalline dodecaboride intergranular phase was generated upon cooling to ameliorate the adhesion between the components. The as-sintered composite presents a high hardness of 36.4 GPa at a load of 0.49 N and 24.4 GPa at a load of 9.8 N. This liquid phase–assisted rapid ultrahigh-temperature strategy can be widely applicable for other ultrahigh-temperature ceramics as well.
